newsitem.title: USA: Hydro-Quebec CEO sees one N.American power market.
newsitem.headline: Hydro-Quebec CEO sees one N.American power market.

text.p: The head of Hydro-Quebec, Canada's giant power producer, sees deregulation rapidly erasing the line between the U.S. and Canadian electricity markets, leaving behind one vast continental grid.

"I'm convinced there's going to be one North American electricity market. The question is, how long will it take? It is very doubtful it could be 10 years. It will be less," Andre Caille, president and chief executive officer of Hydro-Quebec, told Reuters in an interview Thursday.
Achieving this vision requires vigilant regulation of the market's transition to open competition, a process Caille said he is convinced will succeed.

"There will be no losers. There are regulatory boards there to ensure no groups are hurt," he said, citing the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the Quebec Energy Regulatory Board, established just last year.
Both agencies have mandated open competition among power producers at the wholesale level, a move aimed at lowering power prices to consumers through basic market efficiencies.
This trend is also well advanced in other provinces like British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario.
Caille said Hydro-Quebec intends to aggressively pursue market share in this new environment.
The company owns 31,000 megawatts (MW) of power generation capacity and has access to another 4,000 MW through ventures with companies in Newfoundland and Labrador.
Of this, 94 percent is hydropower, making it the biggest source of hydroelectricty in North America.
With access to so much cheap power, Hydro-Quebec is looking hard at selling its surplus to the U.S. market.
A key step in this direction was its application to FERC for a U.S. electricity marketers license.
"I expect a decision will be made in coming weeks and I am confident the application will be accepted," he said.

On May 1, Hydro-Quebec opened it transmission grid to outside producers and split off its power transmission group as an independent division, a move required by FERC to ensure the company's generation division does not enjoy cheaper transmission rates than outside competitors moving power across their wires.
Caille confirmed Hydro-Quebec's competitive strategy includes actively seeking partners or strategic alliances south of the border.
"We have had discussions with many large and intermediary U.S. marketers, but have not alligned ourselves with any of them yet."

He also said Hydro-Quebec is seriously weighing partnerships at U.S. power plants, especially gas-fired thermal units close to key markets, citing New England, Michigan, and even New York as areas where it would be natural for the company to expand its power sales.

Caille conceded transmission capacity from Hydro-Quebec's plants into the U.S. probably is inadequate to carry the volume of export power he anticipates, and that the company is looking into upgrading existing lines rather than build new corridors.
Hydro-Quebec, with headquarters in Montreal, is fully-owned by the Province of Quebec.
Its assets total nearly US$40 billion, with annual revenues of nearly US$6 billion, about 12 percent of which is earned outside the province.
((--New York Power Desk 212 859 1621))
